extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in discrete and combinatorial geometry
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedia-style summary of Borsuk's problem in discrete geometry: its statement, historical positive results, counterexamples, bounds on the function α(n), and related questions about bodies of constant width.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk problem (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can every bounded subset E of R^n be partitioned into (n+1) sets, each of which has a smaller diameter than E?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central question (historically called Borsuk's conjecture). The page frames this as asking whether every bounded set in Euclidean n-space can be decomposed into n+1 pieces each of strictly smaller diameter than the original set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of α(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: α(n) denotes the minimal number of pieces needed so that every bounded subset of R^n can be partitioned into α(n) sets of smaller diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the research is concerned with the behavior of α(n): whether α(n) = n+1 for all n (the original question), or how α(n) grows with n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive (proved) cases where n+1 pieces suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: There are classes/dimensions for which the answer is positive: n = 2 (Borsuk's original result), n = 3 (Perkal, Eggleston, later simpler proofs by Grünbaum and Heppes), and for all n in certain classes of sets such as smooth convex bodies (Hadwiger), centrally-symmetric bodies (A. S. Riesling), and bodies of revolution (Boris Dekster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these as special cases where partition into n+1 smaller-diameter sets is known to be possible; each result references the specific author and year for the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kahn–Kalai counterexample (general disproof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kahn and Kalai (1993) constructed finite sets showing the general answer is no: their construction claimed n+1 pieces do not suffice for n = 1325 and for each n > 2014. (A later correction/clarification by Bernulf Weißbach and subsequent checks verified a counterexample for n = 1325 and for higher dimensions up to 1560.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first major disproof showing Borsuk's conjecture fails in high dimensions; the page notes an initial error in the original numerical claim and the subsequent fixes/confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements on dimensions for counterexamples (Hinrichs & Richter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinrichs and Richter (2003) constructed finite sets for n ≥ 298 which cannot be partitioned into n+11 parts of smaller diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their work improved the bounds on dimensions where the conjecture fails, showing stronger lower bounds on the required number of pieces (n+11 in this construction) for moderately high dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bondarenko and Jenrich two-distance counterexamples (64 and 65 dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bondarenko (2013) showed Borsuk's conjecture is false for all n ≥ 65. Thomas Jenrich soon derived a 64-dimensional counterexample from Bondarenko's construction, giving the best bound at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results significantly lowered the dimension threshold for known counterexamples; Jenrich produced an explicit 64-dimensional two-distance counterexample that was later published with Brouwer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kahn–Kalai lower bound on α(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sufficiently large n, Kahn and Kalai show a superpolynomial lower bound on α(n); the article records a lower bound of the form α(n) ≥ (1.2)^{√n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides asymptotic information: for large dimensions the number of pieces required grows (their construction gives exponential-in-√n growth). The page also notes the correct order of magnitude of α(n) is still unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schramm's upper bound on α(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oded Schramm proved an upper bound: for every ε, if n is sufficiently large then α(n) ≤ (√(3/2) + ε)^{n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an exponential-in-n upper bound on α(n). The article cites Schramm's bound to show α(n) is at most exponentially large in n (with base close to √(3/2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjectured exponential growth (open conjecture about α(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is conjectured that there exists a constant c > 1 such that α(n) > c^n for all n ≥ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records this as an open expectation about the true growth rate of α(n) — that it might be exponential in n rather than subexponential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schramm's effective radius and the rn question for constant-width bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body K of constant width 2, define the effective radius r_n by Vol(K) = r_n^n Vol(B_n). Schramm proved a lower bound sqrt(3 + 2/(n+1)) - 1 ≤ r_n and asked whether there exists ε > 0 such that r_n ≤ 1 - ε for all n ≥ 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a related quantitative question about volumes of constant-width bodies: whether the gap between smallest and largest constant-width bodies grows exponentially with dimension. The page reports a 2024/2025 preprint by Arman, Bondarenko, Nazarov, Prymak, Radchenko giving a construction with Vol(K) ≤ (0.9)^n Vol(B_n), which is presented as an affirmative resolution of this type of question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related problems and conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Connections to Hadwiger's conjecture (covering convex bodies with smaller copies of themselves) and references to the Kahn–Kalai conjecture and other survey/expository works on the Borsuk partition problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article situates Borsuk's problem within a web of related questions in convex and discrete geometry and points to further reading and surveys for broader context.
